findings.text: Where an enterprise depends on institutional bank loans or government tender based supply contracts, delays in obtaining the factory licence carry a direct financial cost, since loan disbursement or billing cannot begin until the licence and pollution clearance are in place, adding to the interest cost burden while the applicant waits.

Smaller enterprises without dedicated technical staff often need to engage a consultant for factory layout drawings and technical paperwork, at a cost of roughly ₹30,000, specifically to avoid documentation errors and repeated queries.

Beyond the consultant's fee, machinery and equipment must meet specifications required under the factory licence, so units incur purchase cost to meet the compliance standard, separate from what they would otherwise spend to build production capacity.
Local telecom and internet infrastructure in industrial belts can occasionally stall online submissions, particularly during heavy monsoons.

Statutory obligations such as ambulance or crèche provisions apply only once workforce thresholds are crossed (e.g., above 500 workers); participants felt Daman/DNH does not offer the kind of graduated, tiered compliance timeline that some other states extend to newer or lower-risk units to phase in such obligations.

Consultants engaged for factory licensing are not officially empanelled or registered with the department, unlike architects (OBPS portal) or water-compliance auditors in the same regulatory ecosystem, leaving service quality and accountability inconsistent.
The application process is almost entirely online; participants did not report using an offline route.
The department publishes a clear checklist on its portal, and once listed documents are ready, completing and submitting the application takes about 30-45 minutes.
Physical inspection is not required for standard, self-declaration based (typically Green category) factory licensing; inspection becomes necessary only for higher-risk (Orange/Red) categories.

Participants described a deemed-approval provision for factory licensing: if the department neither raises a query nor takes any action within 25 days of submission, the application is treated as approved by default.
Related industry services — Factory Licensing, Pollution Control Clearance, Town Planning, and Power — are accessible through the National Single Window Portal.

No redundant or duplicate documentation was reported; participants described the checklist (building layout drawings, land ownership/title records, rent or purchase agreement, fire department permission) as clear and non-repetitive.
Delays occur mainly when the department raises a query due to incomplete documentation; the processing clock pauses until the applicant responds.
Categories where physical inspection is mandated (Orange/Red) take slightly longer — up to around 25 days — compared with standard self-declaration applications not subject to a site visit.

Introduce a transition period along the lines of Gujarat's practice, where green/low-risk category units may commence operations on self-declaration/intimation, with up to two to three years to complete peripheral compliances after operations start.
Strengthen telecom and internet infrastructure in industrial belts to prevent monsoon-related connectivity outages from stalling online submissions.
Consider formal empanelment or registration of consultants engaged for factory licensing, comparable to the registration required of architects or certified water-compliance auditors.
Participants described the department's officers and online portals as responsive and supportive, communicating via SMS, email, and dedicated departmental WhatsApp groups.
Larger organisations with dedicated HR/admin teams tend to process applications in-house, while smaller enterprises more often rely on consultants to avoid clerical errors and repeated queries.

Statutory fees are calculated automatically on the portal based on connected electrical load (HP/KW), number of workers, and pollution category (Green/Orange/Red); participants cited an example fee of roughly ₹22,000, with no hidden charges reported.

Businesses whose activity falls outside standard retail trade need more than the trade license to open: petroleum-related outlets, food service establishments, and salons were all cited as requiring additional clearances.

Trade license fees vary by category rather than a flat rate: the Daman Municipal Council's schedule ranges from roughly ₹1,000 for a hair-cutting salon up to ₹40,000 for higher-risk categories such as a distillery, with restaurants, petrol/CNG dealers, and cafes each positioned at their own point on that scale.
Food service businesses are subject to a second layer of approval, requiring Health Department/Food Inspector clearance in addition to the municipal trade license itself.
The 'deemed approval' concept raised in the discussion aligns with the UT's own time-bound service delivery framework under the Public Service Guarantee Act / Samay Sudhini Seva provisions.

The process includes an inspection step for at least some applications, as referenced in the discussion.

Applications go into a 'pending' state when flagged as incomplete, leaving the applicant to notice, correct, and resubmit the issue.

Sharpen rejection messaging and status visibility, so applicants have clarity on what 'pending' status means and exactly what needs correction.
Combine the municipal and Health Department requirements into a single checklist for food service, personal care, and other sector-linked trades.
Publicise the time-bound/deemed-approval protections already provided under the UT's service guarantee rules, so applicants know the option exists.

The process is routed entirely online through the DMC/municipal portal, with no offline option currently available.

Approval confirmation typically takes roughly four to five days when documentation is in order, though timelines were also said to stretch to fifteen or twenty days, and sometimes close to a month, during busier periods such as April.
Rejected or incomplete submissions are flagged back to the applicant, typically by message and sometimes by phone call, leaving the applicant to correct and resubmit.
Field inspections fall on an unpredictable schedule (one participant linked visits to the period after Republic Day rather than a fixed calendar) and can surface issues such as a lapsed licence.
The same documentation is carried over at renewal where business name, ownership, and location are unchanged; a change in ownership or registered name requires fresh documentation.
Applicants resubmit essentially the same rent/property paperwork at every annual renewal for an unchanged business, a recurring source of friction even though the underlying facts had not changed.
Turnaround can stretch from a matter of days to several weeks during specific periods (April among them) due to backlog, with document rejections requiring correction and resubmission.
Inspections can surface related issues, such as a licence found to have lapsed at the time of a field visit, which participants connected to penalty exposure.
Publish a transparent, category- and size-based fee schedule so businesses understand upfront how their renewal charge is calculated.
Reintroduce or formalise an offline channel alongside the online portal for applicants less comfortable with a fully digital filing process.
Communicate the deemed-approval safeguard proactively so applicants know they have recourse if DMC doesn't act within its own stated timeline.

Provide a single, sector-specific checklist of NOCs and supporting documents (e.g., fire NOC or equipment-related requirements) so businesses know what applies to their trade category before they begin.
Consider a simplified renewal path for businesses with no change in ownership or premises, skipping re-upload of identical property documentation every year.

Participants referenced the differential between DNH's power tariffs and those in neighbouring Maharashtra and Gujarat, and noted that recent tariff revisions combined with rising land costs are seen as narrowing DNH's earlier locational advantage — raised as a broader cost-of-doing-business factor rather than one tied specifically to the CTE process.

findings.text: For MSME participants, obtaining CTE in practice leaves little alternative to hiring an external consultant, since most small units have no dedicated in-house compliance function; one participant's consultant was found through informal, word-of-mouth referral.

Beyond the consultant's fee, the bylaws attached to the checklist prescribe specific equipment, machinery, and record-keeping, so units incur cost simply to satisfy the compliance standard, independent of what the plant would otherwise need for production.

A related cost is the salary paid to technical and managerial staff engaged ahead of commissioning to prepare and pursue the application; this cost accrues from hiring through to approval, even though the staff's time is not yet contributing to production.
Specific equipment, machinery, and documentation items prescribed by the bylaws attached to the CTE checklist are mandatory — a unit cannot substitute a lower-cost alternative even where one exists.

Participants referred to the differential between DNH's power tariffs and those in neighbouring Maharashtra and Gujarat, and to how recent tariff revisions combined with rising land costs are narrowing DNH's earlier locational advantage.

CTE is granted by the Pollution Control Committee (PCC); the process includes a mandatory physical inspection in addition to document review, with queries logged and resolved online before the application can proceed.
At the renewal stage, a fresh sample analysis is required as part of consent renewal, separate from what is submitted at the original establishment stage.

Units are classified by pollution potential (Green/White/Orange/Red); a zero-discharge unit with no liquid effluent was exempted from the Effluent Treatment Plant requirement applicable to units generating liquid effluent.

Lower-risk (White category) units are not processed any faster: the same sequence of document review, portal-based query resolution, and mandatory site inspection applies irrespective of category, so procedural timelines end up comparable to higher-risk units despite a materially lighter environmental review burden.
Participants described having to respond to repeated document requests as applications moved through the portal, though no specific duplicate document or resubmission instance was named.

Delay was attributed less to any single step and more to the cumulative effect of sequential requirements: the mandatory field inspection, portal-based queries each needing resolution, and for MSMEs, added turnaround from routing documentation through an external consultant.

Land carrying cost, machinery investment, and pre-commissioning staff salaries continue to accrue regardless of how quickly regulatory steps clear, making the inspection/query cycle a meaningful driver of pre-operational cost even though CTE itself was typically granted within roughly 30-45 days.
Ensure deemed-approval provisions function automatically as designed, rather than still requiring a separate explicit sign-off from the department.
Introduce differentiated, faster processing for lower-risk (Green/White category) units so procedural timelines reflect their comparatively lighter environmental review burden.
The online application portal was described as intuitive enough that a well-prepared applicant could complete the upload in about two hours without consultant assistance.

Consultant fees for CTE filings were cited at roughly ₹20,000-25,000 (composite, inclusive of GST/paperwork), lower than metro rates; statutory fees scale with capital investment, roughly ₹25,000/year or ₹1,25,000 for a five-year consent tenure for smaller units.

Fear of non-compliance was cited as the reason smaller entrepreneurs continue to rely on external consultants, whereas larger corporates absorb this function through dedicated in-house legal and compliance teams.
Participants also raised operational challenges outside CTE itself, including local labour retention and workforce stability, as factors affecting overall ease of doing business.

findings.text: GSTR-2B reflects only on the 14th while GSTR-3B is due on the 20th, leaving about six days (sometimes around three working days where a weekend falls before the due date) to reconcile purchases, a manual check for businesses with thousands of monthly invoices.

ITC can be claimed only to the extent it shows in GSTR-2B; credit shown in the books as receivable is lost to the buyer if a supplier files GSTR-1 late or not at all, even where the invoice is genuine and the supplier has been paid.

Notices arrive months, and in one reference about two years later, asking the buyer to reverse ITC with interest and penalty because the supplier did not deposit the tax, felt unfair to a buyer who had paid in full.

Correcting an invoice is difficult: cancellation is possible only within 24 hours; after that the only route is a credit note, and if the recipient does not accept it, the supplier still has to pay the tax even though the value can be reversed in the accounts.

Manpower is a hidden compliance cost: larger businesses (turnover up to around ₹1,000 crore mentioned) may need four to five dedicated staff for dispatch/invoicing (including e-way bills), accounts/purchase entry, and return filing/reconciliation, while a small business can manage with one.

Recurring portal problems: the portal is slow at times, and during annual return (GSTR-9) filing, data (e.g., Table 8A) does not auto-populate properly, so tickets have to be raised repeatedly and are often closed as resolved without a fix, sometimes close to the due date with penalty exposure; ITC on imports was also said not to reflect at times.

E-way bill generation is repetitive: a separate bill has to be created for every invoice even to the same party, and product-wise invoicing on customer request (ten to fifteen items becoming ten to fifteen invoices) multiplies e-way bills.

The law keeps changing — ITC eligibility, reversals and rates revised often — making compliance more complicated even though filing itself is easier; new joiners may not know requirements such as reverse charge (RCM), and several participants felt GST has moved away from its original 'one tax, one return, one process' promise.

A key policy concern: the recipient bears the consequence of a supplier's default. Participants argued the department should recover tax from the defaulting supplier rather than reverse the buyer's credit with interest and penalty — reportedly expected to be taken up at the last GST Council meeting but not decided.

ITC is allowed only once goods are received, so an invoice dated at month-end for goods still in transit shifts to the following month's credit, creating month-to-month mismatches that participants found hard to manage.
Where a business pays input tax at a higher rate than output tax (inverted duty structure), credit accumulates in the ledger and can only be recovered through a refund, described as the sole option.

Job work movements need an e-way bill regardless of the ₹50,000 value threshold that applies to other goods; participants suggested extending the distance limit for local movement of goods between Daman and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
No government fee or delay cost was reported for filing, and no other substantive cost was reported for the filing process itself.

Returns are filed online on the GST portal in a monthly cycle (GSTR-1 ~11th, GSTR-2B 14th, GSTR-3B with payment by 20th; GSTR-9 annually); filed in-house via software (e.g., ClearTax) or through consultants, and the mechanics of filing were described as having become easier.

Because the portal does not reconcile purchases against GSTR-2B automatically, matching is done manually or via third-party software, and a supplier's late GSTR-1 filing leaves the corresponding credit missing from GSTR-2B at the time of filing.

When a supplier amends a GSTIN on an invoice, the amended entry shows only in the next month's GSTR-2B, and the buyer is not alerted to the change; participants must identify and explain such amendments later, including during a government audit.
Reconciling the same purchase data recurs monthly and again at the annual return stage; supplier amendments must be explained afresh during an audit even though the department already holds the data.
Support tickets often need several attempts before a problem is actually resolved, which becomes critical when it coincides with a due date.

Allow ITC to a buyer who holds a valid invoice and has genuinely paid the supplier, and recover tax directly from the supplier who has not deposited it, rather than reversing the buyer's credit with interest and penalty.
Provide more time for ITC reconciliation (e.g., earlier GSTR-2B availability or a wider 14th-to-20th window) and introduce an auto-reconciliation facility on the portal.
Reduce the frequency of changes in ITC eligibility, reversal and rate rules, and simplify the law to move closer to one tax, one return, one process.

Allow one e-way bill to cover multiple invoices to the same party, review the e-way bill requirement for job work, and extend the distance limit for local movement of goods between Daman and Dadra and Nagar Haveli.
